desc:
You are given a string s and an integer k. In one move you choose one of the first k letters of the current string (all letters if the string is shorter than k), remove it and append it to the end of the string. You may make any number of moves, including none.

Return the lexicographically smallest string you can end up with.

s = "cba", k = 1    -> "acb"
s = "baaca", k = 3  -> "aaabc"
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Start with k = 1. What strings can you reach by moving the first letter to the back again and again?
With k = 1 you can only rotate the string, so try every rotation. With k = 2, think about whether you can swap two neighbouring letters (using the extra letter as a helper).
For k ≥ 2 adjacent letters can be exchanged, which means any permutation is reachable, so the answer is simply the sorted string. For k = 1 take the smallest rotation.
editorial: If k = 1 the only operation is to move the first letter to the back, which rotates the string. The reachable strings are exactly its n rotations, and the answer is the smallest of them. Building all rotations costs O(n2) which is fine here; Booth's algorithm or the minimal-rotation trick does it in O(n).

If k ≥ 2 we can pick the second letter as well. Think of the string as a circle with a pointer at its start. Moving the first letter to the back just advances the pointer. Moving the second letter to the back takes y out of x y rest and gives x rest y; read as a circle this is y x rest with the pointer at x, so x and y have exchanged places. Pointer moves are free and every neighbouring pair can be brought to the front, so any two adjacent letters can be exchanged. Adjacent exchanges generate every ordering of the letters, so the sorted string is reachable, and nothing is smaller than the sorted order.
So: return sorted(s) when k > 1, and the minimum rotation when k = 1.
time: O(n^2) for k = 1, O(n log n) otherwise
